A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MV-RoboBench. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained examples across relocation and terminology changes.

before.justification: Tables 2–3 report original model evaluations, augmentation experiments and human performance. Appendix D also identifies the authors' OmniSpatial reproductions.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by ERQA evaluations, single-view ablations, orientation and rejection tests, and qualitative model-error analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix C.3 changes the described VGGT augmentation from four synthesized views per original camera pair to one interpolated frame per pair, a limited inference-input revision. The benchmark construction and the prompting, scene-description and depth-augmentation approaches otherwise remain.

E1.justification: The AgiWorld/BridgeV2 benchmark and OmniSpatial evaluation remain. v2 adds ERQA embodied-reasoning evaluation and distinct single-view, inverted-image and absent-correct-answer scenarios, substantially broadening evaluated input conditions and task requirements.

E2.justification: The comparator rosters in the matched MV-RoboBench, augmentation and OmniSpatial experiments are unchanged. New evaluations reuse subsets of existing models; the single-view controls alter input conditions rather than introduce another comparator method.

E3.justification: Appendices G–I introduce a four-task single-view protocol using AgiWorld's head camera or BridgeV2 view1, inversion of non-gripper images, and a seven-task rejection test with the correct answer always at option E. Appendix C.3 revises the synthesized-view count, while Figure 3 corrects five AgiWorld subtask counts without changing the stated total of 1,708. These reported revisions do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–J investigate multi-view necessity, orientation sensitivity, rejection of invalid choices and recurring model failures. The qualitative analysis examines 10–20 erroneous cases per model for GPT-5 and two Qwen models, with three illustrated case studies. These substantially extend the retained augmentation analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions state that question order and random seeds are fixed across runs and report average accuracy from five human participants. Neither supplies model-run counts, confidence intervals, dispersion estimates or formal significance tests. The new accuracy deltas do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain identical numerical entries. v2 adds extensive results under new conditions: GPT-5 scores 59.34% on ERQA, 37.68% under inverted images and 13.43% on the seven-task rejection test. Single-view comparisons and qualitative failure findings are also new, and Figure 3 corrects five counts downward by one. Table 7's single-/multi-view labeling is inconsistent with the corresponding Table 2 values.

T1.justification: Appendix E.3 retains the same gravity-anchored, right-handed coordinate definitions and equations, and the spatial task retains its 5 × 5 × 5 grid. No substantive mathematical definition, theorem, proof or derivation is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the benchmark's scope and novelty claim, the human-performance gap, positive spatial–robotic correlation and weak transfer from general single-view benchmarks. The new analyses do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking multi-view benefits to reasoning capacity, orientation sensitivity to upright-image bias, and weak-model stability to floor effects. It interprets rejection failures as over-compliance, develops detailed failure mechanisms, discusses mitigation through camera orientation control, and newly argues that ERQA has limited discriminative power.

D1.justification: New Appendix E.5 documents annotator qualifications and training, approximately 200/600/400 hours across construction stages, hard-distractor design and independent cross-checking. v2 also discloses 224 × 224 synthesized inputs, depth normalization and Gaussian smoothing, permitted external references during human evaluation, and additional project/data links. These mostly expand documentation rather than establish changed underlying procedures.

R1.justification: Table 1 and the introduction add ERQA and MMSI-Bench comparisons, including their partial multi-view coverage. Appendices add HSSBench, EgoBrain and two diffusion-related citations. The existing related-work organization and central research positioning remain largely intact.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering remain intact. v2 locally rewrites Appendices B–C and parts of F, simplifies some terminology, updates front matter, adds ethics and reproducibility statements, and extends the appendix organization to accommodate the new material.

P2.justification: v2 adds four experimental tables (Tables 5 and 7–9) and three illustrated model-error cases (Figures 29–31), substantially expanding the quantitative and qualitative displays. Table 1 expands, retained task examples receive revised captions and placement, and headers, hyperlinks and code-listing presentation change.

improvement.justification: The annotation documentation, corrected dataset counts and targeted controls/error analyses improve transparency and diagnostic value. However, Table 7 labels apparent single-view scores as multi-view: GPT-5's 36.32 plus the reported 18.90 difference equals Table 2's 55.22. The rejection test also fixes every correct answer at E, leaving answer-position effects unresolved. These reporting and design issues limit the net quality gain.
